conceptTag: Rebuild a product's cost from scratch
readerTitle: What is a $18 cutting board actually made of?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (선물 가게의 도마, 식당의 하우스 드레싱) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 공급가는 남이 정한 숫자일 뿐이다. 부품부터 원가를 다시 쌓으면 협상 근거가 생긴다. 다만 그 숫자는 바닥값이므로 안전 여유를 더해서 계획해야 한다.
misconception: 원가를 처음부터 계산하면 그 숫자가 곧 내가 낼 수 있는 진짜 가격이다. 비교는 다른 공급업체 견적끼리만 하면 된다.

factChecks.note: 도마 계산: 목재 $3 + 가공 $3 + 오일·라벨 $0.50 + 운송 $1.50 = $8.00. 유통가 $18과의 차이는 $10.
드레싱 계산: 재료 리터당 $3, 조리 인건비 시급 $20 × 15분 ÷ 4리터 = 리터당 $1.25, 합계 $4.25. 구매가 $12/리터.

cards.title: What is a $18 cutting board actually made of?
body: Mina runs a small gift shop. Her best seller is a wooden cutting board. She buys it from a distributor for $15 and sells it for $35.
This month the distributor's new price list says $18. Mina picks up a board and turns it over. It's a piece of wood, some oil and a paper label.

image.label: A shop owner holding a wooden cutting board next to a price list
image.brief: 따뜻한 조명의 작은 선물 가게 계산대. 주인이 나무 도마를 뒤집어 보고 있고, 옆에 "$15"에 줄이 그어지고 "$18"로 바뀐 가격표 종이. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 넣지 않음.

cards.title: The price just went up 20%.
body: Mina's margin on the board shrinks from $20 to $17. She wants to respond before her next order.

options.text: Get quotes from two other distributors and pick the cheapest
options.feedback: Useful, but she'd only compare one price list with another. If all distributors charge around $18, she learns nothing about what the board should cost.

options.text: Work out what the board costs to make, part by part
options.feedback: This is **first principles thinking**: break the product into parts whose costs you can check. It gives her a number that doesn't come from anyone's price list.

options.text: Raise her shelf price to $38 and move on
options.feedback: Fast, and it protects her margin for now. But she accepts the new cost without knowing whether it's fair, and her customers pay for it.

cards.title: Mina calls a local woodworking shop.
body: Built from parts, the board comes to about **$8**. The distributor charges $18. That $10 gap isn't all profit. It pays for their storage, sales staff and returns. But now Mina knows what she's paying for.
cards.softwareNote: Software teams can do the same with a tool they pay for per seat. List what it actually does for you, then price each piece: hosting, the features you use, support. You may find you pay for far more than you need.

cards.title: A price list is someone else's answer.
body: The $18 started with the distributor's costs and goals, then got rounded to what the market accepts. Comparing it with other distributors only checks one guess against another.
**First principles** means going down to things you can verify: what the wood costs, what an hour of sanding costs, what a van trip costs. Those facts don't depend on anyone's price list.
Even if Mina never switches suppliers, she now has an honest number to negotiate with.

cards.title: Mina is ready to order direct.
body: The workshop agrees to make boards for her. The minimum order is 100 boards, paid upfront. She's drafting her plan.
Which cost per board should she plan with?

options.feedback: It's the best case. Any warped board, late delivery or hour she spends checking stock pushes the real cost above it. A plan built on the floor price breaks easily.

options.text: About $11: $8 plus allowances for defects, her time and a cushion
options.feedback: This is a **margin of safety**: plan with a number that still works when things go wrong. At $11 she still saves $7 a board against $18.

options.text: Stay with the distributor. Going direct is too risky
options.feedback: It avoids the upfront cash and the hassle. But she gives up a likely $7 a board, and she's ignoring a number she just worked to find.

cards.title: The number you rebuild is always too low.
body: A cost built from parts leaves out the work that holds the parts together. Lists are tidy. Real life adds:
list: **Defects:** some boards crack or arrive stained
**Cash tied up:** 100 boards paid weeks before they sell
**Your time:** ordering, checking and chasing late deliveries
**Lost services:** the distributor took returns and kept stock for you
cards.callout: Use the scratch number to question a price. Add a margin before you bet on it.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant's house dressing.
body: A restaurant buys its house dressing ready-made at $12 a litre. The chef rebuilds the cost. Oil, vinegar, mustard and herbs come to about $3 a litre. A cook paid $20 an hour makes 4 litres in 15 minutes, which adds $1.25 a litre.

options.text: Switch today. $4.25 against $12 is an easy win
options.feedback: The first-principles math is right, but $4.25 has no margin. Spoiled batches, a busy cook skipping prep or a taste that changes from day to day would all eat into the savings.

options.text: Plan at about $6 a litre to cover waste and busy days, and test it for a month
options.feedback: **First principles** found the gap. A **margin of safety** keeps the plan realistic. A short test shows whether the cushion is big enough before the restaurant drops its supplier.

options.text: Keep buying. It's only a dressing
options.feedback: Fair if the restaurant uses very little, since the savings may not be worth the effort. At larger volumes, it's leaving real money on the table every week.

cards.softwareNote: The same check applies to building a tool in-house instead of paying for it. Developer time is easy to count. Bug fixes, updates and the person who leaves are the costs that need a margin.

cards.title: Rebuild the cost, then add a cushion.
body: Break a product into parts you can price yourself. Then plan with a number that survives a bad week.
**Try it today:** pick one thing you buy in bulk. List its parts and price each one. Compare the total with what you pay, then add 30% and compare again.
list: **First principles** (THK-01-01): price the parts, not the price list
**Margin of safety** (THK-01-05): plan above the floor so mistakes don't sink the plan
